title: Webb Telescope Releases One of Its Largest Images, Revealing Record-Breaking Brown Dwarfs
summary:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has released one of its largest panoramas to date — a breathtaking view of IC 348, a star-forming reflection nebula about 1,000 light-years away in the constellation Perseus. The image, shared on September 15, 2026, shows an intricate landscape of young stars, glowing gas, and sweeping clouds of dust.

IC 348 is one of the closest stellar nurseries to Earth. In the near-infrared image, bright stars display JWST's distinctive diffraction spikes, while still-forming protostars in the upper-right launch jets of material. These jets, known as Herbig-Haro objects, can stretch trillions of miles into space.

But the most remarkable discovery hides in the dust: brown dwarfs — substellar objects that are heavier than giant gas planets like Jupiter but never become hot enough to fuse hydrogen into helium. Sometimes called "failed stars," they form the same way as regular stars, through the collapse of molecular clouds, but their cores never ignite.

In 2024, researchers used Webb's NIRCam instrument to survey part of IC 348 and found 39 brown dwarf candidates. The following year, Webb's NIRSpec instrument studied the light of 15 of them. Nine were confirmed as new substellar members of the cluster. The faintest is estimated to have a mass of around two Jupiters — making it the least massive brown dwarf ever found.

How small the smallest brown dwarf can be is an open question in astrophysics. This discovery helps researchers constrain the limits of how tiny these strange objects can get.

The image also captures gravitational lensing, where distant galaxies' light is distorted by foreground mass, and even spiral galaxies in the background. IC 348 was recently observed by NASA's Chandra Observatory as well, which captured the nursery in X-ray light.

Jamie Carter, a Cardiff-based science journalist, notes that this is just one tiny detail in one of JWST's biggest images yet — a reminder of how much the telescope can reveal.
why_it_matters: Objects that sit between planets and stars force astronomers to decide where the categories they use break down, and that matters for how we classify planets, brown dwarfs and stars everywhere in the universe. Publishing one of the telescope's largest images also shows how public, shared observatories turn raw data into questions the whole field can chase.

background_read: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), launched in 2021, is the largest infrared telescope ever flown; it orbits the Sun about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth and can see through dust that blocks visible light.
Brown dwarfs were only confirmed as a class of object in the 1990s. They sit in the fuzzy gap between planets and stars, and astronomers still argue about how the smallest ones manage to form at all.

The constellation Perseus is a pattern of stars named after a hero of Greek mythology; because it looks toward a nearby cloud of gas and dust, it has become a favourite hunting ground for young stars and brown dwarfs.
NASA's Chandra Observatory, launched in 1999 and named after the astrophysicist Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, studies the sky in X-rays — a wavelength that reveals the hot gas around newborn stars.
JWST uses infrared instruments such as NIRCam, which takes images, and NIRSpec, which splits the light of individual objects into a spectrum so that their mass and temperature can be estimated.

perspectives.perspective: Astronomers studying how stars and planets form
perspectives.description: A brown dwarf only about two Jupiter masses in size challenges ideas about how small a star-like object can be, and gives theorists a real test case. JWST's large mosaics let researchers see an entire nursery at once rather than in isolated snapshots.

Masses for faint, cool objects are inferred from models of how they radiate, so a 'two-Jupiter-mass' brown dwarf could carry a large uncertainty. Some of these objects might in fact be planets ejected from their birth orbits, which would change the interpretation entirely.

Brown dwarfs were only confirmed as a class in the 1990s, and the boundary between the heaviest planets and the lightest stars has been blurry ever since. Every new record at the low-mass end is one more data point in a long-running argument about where that boundary sits.

Follow-up spectroscopy plus wider surveys — including X-ray views such as Chandra's — will show whether very low-mass brown dwarfs are common or rare. Finding many more of them could reveal whether they form like stars or like planets.
